pages.description: H.R.5408 would require an employer to begin bargaining soon after its workers vote to form a union. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, the dispute may proceed to federal mediation and, if mediation fails, to an arbitration panel whose decision would be binding.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Compared with the law in force on June 9, 2026, the bill would give newly recognized or certified unions under the National Labor Relations Act deadlines and a binding way to settle stalled first-contract talks. Existing law says bargaining “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1]. The bill adds “mandatory deadlines for parties negotiating an initial collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and provides for mediation and arbitration to finalize CBAs.” [2] Either party could request mediation. If it fails, the bill requires referral to a panel whose decision would be “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [3]. This strengthens workers’ bargaining position against delay: Congress finds that employers use delays “to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” [3]

points.title: It strengthens workers’ route to uncover pollution and enforce environmental safeguards at work.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It strengthens workers’ route to uncover pollution and enforce environmental safeguards at work.

  • Because Union contracts can give workers a regular role in environmental oversight. The 2018 U.S. Steel agreement requires “A Joint Environmental Sub-Committee of the Joint Safety and Health Committee” [4] at each location and says it “will meet regularly to discuss environmental issues affecting the Company and to make appropriate recommendations.” [4]
  • Because The company must let that group review “all non confidential environmental reports, monitoring results, analyses, materials received from the EPA and other agencies” [4].
  • Because The same contract requires the company to “comply with all applicable laws and regulations concerning the health and safety of Employees at work and the protection of the environment.” [4]
  • Because Contract duties have a complaint process: “the Union may process grievances through the grievance procedure, including arbitration” [4]. Its outcome is binding: “A decision of the Board shall be final and binding upon the Company, the Union and all Employees concerned.” [4]
  • So These terms give workers information, a voice and a way to enforce environmental duties. By making first contracts harder to block through delay, the bill strengthens this route to challenging pollution. That serves [NAME]’s wish to protect nature.
points.con_html:
Response The bill’s binding route does not clearly reach environmental oversight terms that lack a direct link to workers’ jobs.

  • Because The PRO’s enforcement route depends on specific contract language. The agreement’s complaint process concerns “a violation by the Company of this Agreement” [4]. Grievances can enforce environmental duties only where those duties are in the contract.
  • Because The PRO’s guide says employers can lawfully refuse talks about optional topics “that lack a direct job nexus.” [5] This means topics without a direct link to workers’ jobs.
  • Because The bill’s panel issues a decision “settling the dispute” [3] based on five business and employment factors, such as “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3]. None names pollution oversight, and the bill does not change which subjects employers must negotiate.
  • So For environmental oversight without a direct job link, the PRO identifies no way the bill’s deadlines or panel get past an employer’s lawful refusal. This response does not answer oversight terms tied to workers’ own safety and health, or the grievance rights a first contract can create for terms it does contain.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [6], [7].

points.title: It strengthens bargaining for protected action against work that threatens the environment.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It strengthens bargaining for protected action against work that threatens the environment.

  • Because Workers can bargain for the right to stop dangerous work: “Under the National Labor Relations Act, health and safety is a mandatory subject of collective bargaining in private sector workplaces.” [8]
  • Because A process negotiated at Delaware City Refining Company gives workers “the authority, without fear of reprimand or retaliation, to immediately STOP any work activity that presents a hazard to you, your co-workers, the environment” [8].
  • Because It protects their income: “there shall be no loss of pay, seniority, or benefits during the period of refusal” [8].
  • So A stronger first-contract process helps workers secure these protections. They let workers act before dangerous work harms nature, without losing pay for intervening. [NAME] values such action to defend the environment.
points.con_html:
Response The required duty to bargain that the PRO cites concerns safety and health; it does not establish a required route to work refusals over hazards to the environment alone.

  • Because The safety guide states the duty in those terms: “the other side must bargain in good faith over safety and health issues, including SWA.” [8] SWA means workers’ authority to stop unsafe work.
  • Because The same guide says the terms vary: “Because there is no law mandating SWA, the SWA process is specific to an employer or workplace.” [8] The environmental wording the PRO cites comes from the Delaware City process.
  • So The PRO moves from a required subject of talks to rights that also cover environmental hazards. The guide does not say environment-only coverage is a required subject. This response does not answer stop-work terms for worker hazards that would also avert environmental harm.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [6], [7].

points.title: It strengthens bargaining for workplace programs that save resources and cut climate pollution.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It strengthens bargaining for workplace programs that save resources and cut climate pollution.

  • Because U.S. employers and unions may agree on climate goals. A guide to green bargaining explains that “employers and unions are still free to bargain over them.” [5]
  • Because The guide’s international contract models include “building efficiency improvements and recycling and composting programs” [5] and “employee transit programs that promote the use of public transportation, bikes, and carpooling.” [5]
  • Because A U.S. example makes the route concrete. U.S. Steel’s contract requires joint work to “identify, analyze, and make recommendations regarding ways to conserve energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions” [4].
  • Because Contracts also fund environmental work. Minneapolis janitors won a “contract that included funding for a Labor-Management Cooperation Fund for a green education initiative” [9].
  • Because Climate pollution harms nature. The IPCC finds that “Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming” [10] and that “Hundreds of local losses of species have been driven by increases in the magnitude of heat extremes” [10].
  • So By strengthening the route to a first agreement, the bill helps workers bargain for environmental programs and resources to carry them out. Saving resources and working to cut the gases that warm the planet serve [NAME]’s care for nature.
points.con_html:
Response For climate commitments treated as optional subjects, the PRO identifies no way the bill’s binding route overcomes an employer’s refusal.

  • Because The green-bargaining guide says employers and unions “are still free to bargain over them.” [5] That passage concerns climate goals treated as optional subjects; it does not require either side to accept talks about them. The guide adds that “making employers bargain over climate change may not always be possible” [5].
  • Because The Supreme Court explains the rule for topics outside wages, hours and other employment terms: “each party is free to bargain or not to bargain, and to agree or not to agree.” [11]
  • Because The bill requires a decision “settling the dispute” [3] based on five business and employment factors, including “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3]. It does not change which subjects employers must negotiate.
  • So Optional climate commitments would still depend on an employer’s voluntary agreement. This response does not answer programs that are themselves terms of employment, or the guide’s separate argument that some climate matters can be required subjects.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [6], [7].

points.title: It supports the people who protect wildlife and habitats.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It supports the people who protect wildlife and habitats.

  • Because Conservation workers face first-contract delays too. Audubon’s first agreement “was reached after more than two years of negotiations” [12].
  • Because Audubon’s agreement links its staff to nature protection: “Audubon is committed to the mission of protecting birds and the habitats needed to sustain them” [13] and “Audubon’s workforce is integral to the success of Audubon’s mission” [13].
  • Because That first contract provides practical support for their skills: “Audubon shall support career development training that enhances the skills necessary to successfully perform the employee’s job or other Audubon career positions by providing paid leave to eligible employees” [13].
  • Because Pay and benefits also support conservation staffing. Defenders of Wildlife tied its bargaining effort to “developing a top-tier benefits package to retain and attract top talent” [14]; the resulting agreement “optimizes staff compensation and establishes new benefits for all current and future staff.” [14]
  • So Giving newly organized conservation staff a binding route through stalled talks supports their efforts to secure pay, benefits and training. Supporting the staff who carry out wildlife and habitat protection serves [NAME]’s value.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Defenders of Wildlife release reports contract terms and management’s goal of retaining and attracting staff. It reports no measured change in retention or conservation capacity. The agreement was fast-tracked in the new chief executive’s first 100 days. Sources: [14].

points.title: It addresses a barrier to moving away from fossil fuels: fear that new jobs will not support workers’ families.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It addresses a barrier to moving away from fossil fuels: fear that new jobs will not support workers’ families.

  • Because Contracts put benefits in writing in electric-vehicle battery jobs. An Ultium worker explained: “now my benefits are guaranteed in writing, ensuring financial security for my family” [15].
  • Because Contracts can also support workers changing jobs: “unions can bargain for employer-sponsored training programs that give employees an opportunity to learn new skills.” [5] They can negotiate “robust severance pay and layoff benefit plans and even early retirement” [5].
  • Because Interviews with 48 union energy workers in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania identified fear of poor pay and benefits as a barrier to backing cleaner energy. The researchers conclude: “This analysis demonstrates that there are ways to gain their support, particularly if training, family sustaining wages and benefits, and location are integrated into transitions.” [16]
  • Because The bill puts family needs into binding contract decisions. A panel must base its decision partly on “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [3].
  • So For clean-energy workplaces that newly organize, a binding route to settling wages and benefits can ease part of the financial insecurity these workers identify. Strengthening that part of the move away from fossil fuels can help build support for cutting the emissions that harm nature.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The energy-worker study interviewed 48 unionized workers, all in the Mid-Atlantic region, and its authors note this limit. The Spring Hill Ultium agreement builds on a national contract; workers there signed cards in September 2024 and ratified a local agreement by March 2025. Sources: [16], [15].

Evidence note: In the energy-worker study, workers cite lower pay and precarity in renewable jobs, and the authors say those industries risk becoming non-union and low-wage. They name training, family-sustaining wages and benefits, and location together, and note particular concern for workers whose skills are not in demand in wind and solar. The study does not measure whether first-contract terms change these workers’ expectations. The bill’s comparator factor refers to other employers in the same business. Sources: [16], [3].

points.title: It protects organizations through which workers can defend nature together.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It protects organizations through which workers can defend nature together.

  • Because First-contract delay puts new unions at risk. Representative Scott explains: “Dragging out negotiations gives corporations a long chance to break up a union.” [17]
  • Because Workers use unions to build environmental alliances. Researchers report that union members active on climate issues have “forged new alliances with other unions and environmentalists” [16].
  • Because These organizations have helped win nature protections: “the AFL-CIO helped establish the National Wilderness Preservation System; the United Auto Workers was the leading funder of the first Earth Day and more recently supported raising emissions standards for autos.” [18]
  • So For workers organizing to defend nature through their union, limiting first-contract delay helps protect a group they can use for that action. Keeping this route to environmental campaigns open serves [NAME]’s value of taking part in nature protection.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The historical environmental actions cited come from national union bodies, and the alliance passage concerns members already active on climate. The same article states that unions face a tension, particularly those whose members work in extractive industries. Sources: [18].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect For first union contracts left unsettled after talks and federal mediation, the bill lets a three-person panel impose terms without a worker approval vote: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3] Under the law in force on June 9, 2026, the duty to bargain “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [11].

points.title: Workers lose a way to insist on contract terms that cut pollution and waste.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Workers lose a way to insist on contract terms that cut pollution and waste.

  • Because Contracts can fund changes in how work is done. Minneapolis janitors won “Funding for a green cleaning initiative to reduce waste and water and energy consumption while transitioning away from toxic chemicals, with the goal of significantly lowering carbon emissions from buildings.” [19]
  • Because Winning those terms required workers to put environmental aims ahead of other benefits. Their bargainers reported: “We ultimately won, but had to compromise on the amount of funding and sacrifice other issues like additional holidays that were important to groups of the members.” [19]
  • Because Workers normally can reject a contract: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [20]
  • Because The employer can start the bill's mediation process after 90 days of talks without the union's consent: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3]
  • Because The panel's five required factors concern the business and workers' living costs and pay. None requires pollution cuts. They include “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [3]
  • So A panel can settle a first contract without pollution-cutting terms that workers would insist on before approving it. Workers cannot reject that result, and changing it during the two-year term requires the employer's written consent. Losing that control puts workers' ability to secure such funding at risk, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Minneapolis janitors bargained a renewal: their contract had expired in December. It illustrates green terms and bargaining trade-offs, not a first-contract vote the bill would bypass. Under current law an employer may implement a final offer after genuine good-faith impasse, and the bill requires maintaining current terms pending agreement. Panel factors can accommodate green work methods even though they do not require pollution cuts. Sources: [21], [22], [3].

points.title: Imposed strike limits can weaken workers' ability to take part in defending nature.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Imposed strike limits can weaken workers' ability to take part in defending nature.

  • Because Employers seek strike bans in first contracts: “One thing you can be sure of when bargaining your first contract: management will demand a contract clause barring strikes while the agreement is in effect.” [23]
  • Because Current law leaves unions free to refuse: “Nothing in the NLRA, however, requires a union to agree to a no-strike clause.” [23] The union can also resist through action: “the union may strike to keep it out of the contract.” [23]
  • Because The bill puts disputed contract terms within the panel's reach. Lawyers reviewing it describe “authority to determine all terms of the parties’ first CBA” [22]—their first union contract.
  • So A panel can impose a strike ban that workers never accepted, putting contract limits on walkouts beyond their control.
  • Because Green demands can concern workers' training and daily tasks. Local 26 sought a “training program for Green Technicians (including $0.20 differential) and expanded use of green cleaning.” [21]
  • Because Strike pressure helps workers press such demands. The janitors' bargainers explained that “the companies will simply try to ignore those demands—unless the union is willing to sacrifice and ultimately strike.” [19]
  • So An imposed strike ban can restrict walkouts used to press work-related green demands. Because [NAME] values taking part in defending nature, protecting this means of collective environmental action gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response A strike-ban clause adds little against the green-demand strikes the PRO cites, because those strikes seek new contract terms.

  • Because The cited green strike took place after a contract expired: “The janitors’ contract ran out in December, but they agreed to go on working while negotiations progressed.” [21] The bill's arbitration rule covers “an initial collective bargaining agreement” [3], and its award binds “for a period of 2 years” [3].
  • Because Current law already limits strikes to rewrite terms fixed by an existing contract. The NLRB's guide says: “The party must continue in full force and effect, without resorting to strike or lockout, all the terms and conditions of the existing contract until 60 days after the notice to the other party was given or until the date the contract is scheduled to expire, whichever is later.” [24] This concerns changing agreed terms, not every strike during a contract.
  • So For demands to add green contract terms, the PRO has not shown what a ban clause adds beyond these existing limits. This response does not answer two things: an award itself ends the first-contract bargaining in which workers could strike for such terms, and a ban could reach walkouts not aimed at changing contract terms.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A law-firm analysis in the PRO’s packet says the bill leaves open the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during first-contract talks, and that interest arbitration elsewhere typically rests on a mutual commitment against them. Sources: [22].

points.title: The bill gives unions that fight pollution controls a new way to secure their membership and funding.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill gives unions that fight pollution controls a new way to secure their membership and funding.

  • Because Binding first-contract arbitration can help new unions obtain contracts: “Other research has found that first-contract arbitration helped more Canadian workers sign first contracts.” [25]
  • Because Coal organizing is one use for this route. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) says: “We are going to continue working to organize coal miners, but we must also look outside of the coal industry to grow our membership for a sustainable future” [26]. It also explains why growth matters: “To survive in the long term, we must grow our membership.” [26]
  • Because Contracts can arrange regular collection of members' dues, the payments that fund unions: “provisions that require management to automatically deduct union dues from workers’ paychecks and route them into the labor organization’s account.” [27]
  • So The bill's route to binding contracts can give unions organizing coal and other fossil-fuel workers a firmer base of members and dues income.
  • Because A larger foothold in oil and gas can strengthen the stake in defending those industries. Writing about California politics, Capital & Main reports: “When unions organize workers in the oil and gas industry, they develop a vested interest in protecting those jobs — and can form a serious barrier to environmental justice and climate policy.” [28]
  • Because These unions already turn resources into political pressure. CalMatters reports: “The building and construction trade unions also have long bankrolled California’s labor-friendly Democrats.” [29]
  • Because That pressure has helped defeat environmental limits. CalMatters reports that “Ventura County voters sided with the oil and gas industry and the building trades unions when they overturned similar restrictions the county board of supervisors had placed on local oil wells” [29].
  • Because Coal unions also fight emissions limits in court. In its 2024 challenge to carbon-emission standards for coal-fired power plants, the UMWA stated: “We therefore have no choice but to file this petition, suing the EPA and stopping this rule from ever being implemented.” [30]
  • So Helping these unions sustain members and income can strengthen organized resistance to pollution controls. That risk works against [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature from pollution and gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Canadian first-contract research is reported for workers generally, not by industry. Capital & Main attributes the California building trades’ refinery position to a 2014 state apprenticeship law and a Project Labor Agreement. UMWA’s organizing also includes West Virginia state employees, and state employers are outside the NLRA. Sources: [25], [28], [26], [24].

pages.description: H.R.5408 would require an employer to begin bargaining soon after its workers vote to form a union. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, the dispute may proceed to federal mediation and, if mediation fails, to an arbitration panel whose decision would be binding.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on June 9, 2026, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect The bill adds deadlines, mediation and binding arbitration for a first union contract. Mediation means outside help to reach agreement. Arbitration means a panel decides the terms: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [1] Under the law in force on June 9, 2026, good-faith talks were required, but “it does not impose any deadline or mandate that the parties achieve a collective bargaining agreement.” [2] The bill adds this first-contract process:

  • Because Talks must start within 10 days of a written request, unless both sides agree to more time: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining from an individual or labor organization that has been newly recognized or certified as a representative as provided under section 9(a), or within such further period as the parties agree upon” [1].
  • Because Either side can seek mediation after 90 days without agreement, unless both sides extend that period: “If after the expiration of the 90-day period beginning on the date on which bargaining is commenced, or such additional period as the parties may agree upon, the parties have failed to reach an agreement, either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [1]
  • Because After 30 days from that request without agreement, the mediation service must refer the dispute to a panel, unless both sides extend the time: “If after the expiration of the 30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made under subparagraph (B), or such additional period as the parties may agree upon, the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation, the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].

points.title: It gives workers with less power a way past an employer's use of delay.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives workers with less power a way past an employer's use of delay.

  • Because Treasury's research review explains the power gap: “employers typically have the upper hand in the relationship with their employees, even in the absence of anti-competitive practices.” [3]
  • Because Congress identifies how delay deepens that gap: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” [1]
  • Because The process above lets either side seek a binding settlement. Neither side can block the panel merely by refusing to choose its members: “if the individual or labor organization or the employer fail to do so, the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1]
  • Because Both sides have a place on the panel: “with one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [1]
  • So Workers gain a settlement route beyond persuading the stronger party to agree. Making their right to bargain usable protects people with less power and supports just treatment.
points.con_html:
Response The mediation agency’s documented service limits raise a real question about how quickly and usefully workers with little bargaining power could use the new route.

  • Because The bill depends on the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS): “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].
  • Because FMCS's April 3, 2026 budget submission says it had limited mediation to health-care groups with at least 250 represented workers and “bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction” [4].
  • Because Its proposed service form, published May 15, still says of first-contract cases: “These cases will be assigned to a mediator if they meet the current criteria/metrics for case assignment.” [5]
  • Because A supporter of the bill identifies the practical condition: “Without a robust, government-supported mediation and arbitration system, the Faster Labor Contracts Act would not be able to live up to its promise.” [6]
  • So Preventing an employer from blocking appointments does not resolve this service gap for small units seeking mediation and timely referral. This response does not show that the route is unavailable: the bill’s duty has no size limit, and the time to referral runs from the request.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” Its stated prevalences include grievable safety clauses in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. The bill’s panel factors do not prescribe particular contract terms. Sources: [7], [1].

Brief context note: A review of Canadian first-contract arbitration states that boards and arbitrators limit awards by employer financial capacity and recognize that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. It describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: [8].

points.title: It requires a worker election before the employer's duty to bargain ends.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It requires a worker election before the employer's duty to bargain ends.

  • Because Existing rules allow withdrawal of union recognition after a contract expires when evidence shows lost majority support and the union has not requested an election in time: “If no such petition is timely filed, the employer may rely on the disaffection evidence to affect withdrawal. That evidence—assuming it establishes actual loss of majority status—will be dispositive of the union’s lack of majority status at the time of actual withdrawal; and the withdrawal of recognition will be lawful assuming no other grounds exist to find it unlawful.” [9]
  • Because The bill requires that “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1].

  • So Making such limits more reachable gives workers a way to defend the jobs their households rely on. This protects people vulnerable to losing their income.

points.pro_html:
Point 14 It offers a way to settle first-contract disputes without relying on a strike or lockout.

  • Because Either side can request mediation, followed by a binding decision if talks fail, as set out above.
  • Because Canadian research identifies the bargaining incentive behind this approach: “Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” [14] FCA means first-contract arbitration.
  • Because Stoppages threaten workers' livelihoods: “strikes, lockouts, and other labor disruptions that can be devastating for workers and much more costly to the nation’s economy.” [15]
  • Because Disrupted services also put vulnerable people at risk. Treasury cites research finding that “nurse strikes, though uncommon, lead to diminished patient outcomes” [3].
  • So The bill gives workers an alternative way to seek a first contract and both sides an incentive to settle. Reducing reliance on harmful stoppages protects workers' incomes and people who depend on their services.
points.con_html:
Response The Canadian study does not separate the effect of the settlement incentive from the different legal rules that came with it.

The study notes: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop” [14]. H.R.5408 contains no matching requirement [1]; its command is that the panel “shall render a decision settling the dispute” [1].
  • Because The study says the data do not let it estimate “the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” [14] Here, incidence means how often first-contract strikes or lockouts occur.
  • So The PRO has not shown that the reduction found across those Canadian systems would follow from this bill's settlement route. This response does not answer the narrower point that arbitration gives parties an alternative to relying on a stoppage.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect If in force on June 9, 2026, the bill would let either side request federal mediation after 90 days of first-contract talks. If no agreement follows within 30 days of that request, the federal service must refer the dispute to a three-person panel, unless both sides agree to more time. The panel sets disputed terms: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [1] This is binding arbitration. Current law “does not impose contract terms or set time deadlines for reaching an agreement on a first contract.” [16] The bill also changes the general bargaining rules by requiring parties “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [1] and requiring employers to keep bargaining “absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1].

points.title: It binds workers to terms they cannot reject by voting.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It binds workers to terms they cannot reject by voting.

  • Because Member approval is an existing safeguard under union rules: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [2]
  • Because The bill instead makes the panel’s vote decisive: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute” [1]. Its binding decision requires no approval vote by workers.
  • So Workers bear the consequences of their pay, hours, and workplace rules. Letting them reject terms they judge harmful gives their needs a direct check on the outcome. Removing that safeguard weakens fair treatment in decisions governing their livelihoods.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: A union must represent all employees in the unit fairly and in good faith. Under the bill, the union selects one panel member and the panel must consider employees’ ability to sustain themselves and their families. Sources: [17], [1].

points.title: It pressures workers to settle before they have enough time to understand and press their needs.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It pressures workers to settle before they have enough time to understand and press their needs.

  • Because First-contract talks often involve beginners: “newly unionized employers and newly formed unions are often inexperienced in negotiations.” [2]
  • Because Preparing a first contract requires detailed review of many issues. Labor lawyers explain: “there are too many topics requiring in-depth discussion, negotiation, and drafting to reach agreement in that timeframe.” [18]
  • Because Workers currently use continued bargaining and economic pressure to seek better terms: “workers can use strikes to try to pull employers closer to their demands.” [2]
  • Because The employer can trigger the bill’s route to binding terms despite workers’ objections: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [1] More time requires agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” [1].
  • So Workers cannot keep disputed terms open simply by withholding agreement. An employer can start the move to outside decision-makers while workers still want time to assess proposals or press their demands.
  • Because Representative Fine identifies the resulting pressure: the timetable “increases pressure on workers to settle before they have fully fought for what they deserve.” [19]
  • So Protecting workers who depend on their pay and benefits includes giving them a fair chance to understand and defend those needs. Pressure to accept less before losing direct control threatens that protection.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The bill does not limit the time an arbitration may take once a panel is referred. A review of Ontario cases reports that parties often settle before arbitration concludes and may resume negotiations after an application. The panel must consider the employees’ cost of living. Sources: [2], [8], [1].

points.title: It risks locking workers into safety rules that do not fit their workplace.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It risks locking workers into safety rules that do not fit their workplace.

  • Because The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors warns that arbitrators unfamiliar with a facility could impose “work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations” [20].
  • Because Matching prevention to the workplace matters for worker protection. OSHA explains: “The process described in these recommended practices can, and should, be tailored to the needs of each workplace.” [21]
  • Because The imposed contract lasts two years unless changed by “written consent of the parties.” [1]
  • So A safety rule that misses the workplace’s actual hazards can leave workers exposed to injury. Giving such a rule binding force despite workers’ objections puts the protection of people facing those hazards at risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The panel includes one union-selected and one employer-selected member, and its decision must be based partly on the size and type of the employer’s operations. The FMCS-published arbitrator code says an arbitrator lacking specialized knowledge must decline, withdraw or request technical help, and should comply with a party’s request to visit a work area; the code addresses voluntary arbitration and is applied to agency rosters. A 2009 review says both parties produce evidence to the arbitrator. These warnings and responses cite no record of how arbitrated rules have fit particular workplaces. Sources: [22], [23], [1].

points.title: It risks jobs and livelihoods by letting outsiders impose costs a business cannot sustain.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It risks jobs and livelihoods by letting outsiders impose costs a business cannot sustain.

  • Because A panel can commit a business to costs without its agreement. Representative Walberg warns: “Those contracts could mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain, threaten jobs, kill growth, and in some cases, shut businesses down entirely.” [19]
  • Note The bill requires decisions to consider “the employer's financial status and prospects” [1]. The risk lies in outsiders judging those finances and operations incorrectly. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe warns: “Panel arbitrators may not understand the business” [16].
  • Because A mistaken first contract can shape later ones. Steptoe explains that imposed terms “would set the standard for all future contracts because of the difficulty of unwinding the many complex provisions that go into a collective bargaining agreement.” [16]
  • So Unsustainable costs threaten workers’ jobs and small owners’ livelihoods. Losing that income harms families with little financial cushion and closes opportunities to earn a living. Concern for vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to resist this added risk.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not show why outside decision-makers add a risk of unaffordable costs when the process requires them to examine the business’s finances.

  • Because The award must be based on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [1] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [1]
  • Because Outside decision-makers can apply affordability limits. Slinn and Hurd report that Canadian labor boards and arbitrators have taken “a very conservative approach to first contract awards” [8], limiting them “based on the employer’s financial capacity” [8].
  • So This experience challenges the assumption that an arbitrator’s outside status adds a risk of unaffordable terms. The PRO’s reason is a lawyer’s warning that arbitrators may not understand the business; it offers no example of such an award. Its prediction about later contracts depends on the same claim of added risk in the first contract.

points.title: It puts more strain on public help that poorly funded unions depend on.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 It puts more strain on public help that poorly funded unions depend on.

  • Because The bill adds mandatory mediation and panel-arrangement duties: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [1] After failed mediation, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].
  • Because On June 9, King and MacDonald warned: “The FMCS does not have anywhere near the personnel to meet the obligations this legislation would impose upon it.” [24] FMCS is the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service.
  • Because A June 12 state account of the damage from the 2025 cuts confirms that “the majority of the federal agency’s employees have not returned.” [25]
  • Because Small unions have fewer alternatives. The service is particularly valuable to “small business and small unions that cannot necessarily afford to hire private mediation services.” [15]
  • Because Moving a dispute to a panel does not supply a deadline for finishing it: “The Faster Labor Contracts Act limits the amount of time that can pass before binding arbitration is invoked, but it does not limit the timeline of arbitration.” [2]
  • So Adding compulsory work to a depleted service creates competition for scarce help and another source of delay. Workers whose unions cannot buy private help have fewer ways around that strain. Equal opportunity requires protecting their access to the help needed to secure pay and workplace protections.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect the new mediation and referral duties to a loss of help that poorly funded unions could obtain under current law.

  • Because The staffing report describes already restricted access. Apart from critical-industry and class-action exceptions, negotiation services were limited to employers with “a minimum of 250 employees” [25].
  • Because The bill’s first-contract duty contains no employer-size cutoff: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [1]
  • Because Referral does not wait for completed mediation. The clock is the “30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made” [1]. If agreement has not been reached, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1], unless the parties agree to more time.
  • Because Deciding the contract is the panel’s task, distinct from the service’s mediation and referral work. Existing FMCS practice already uses a separate source of decision-makers: “Arbitrators are not FMCS employees.” [26]
  • So The PRO has not shown how these duties would take help away from poorer unions under the already restricted system. This response does not answer added strain on units that remain eligible for FMCS help, or the absence of a deadline at the panel stage.

points.title: It exposes binding workplace decisions to political influence over appointments.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 It exposes binding workplace decisions to political influence over appointments.

  • Because The bill normally gives each side a panel choice and calls for “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” [1]. But if seats remain unfilled after the 14-day selection period, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1]
  • Because Labor-policy researcher Rachel Greszler warns that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations to hire individuals for arbitrator positions based on their political leanings.” [2]
  • So When the parties cannot fill the seats, federal choices determine who can impose their terms. Selecting arbitrators for their political views threatens workers’ access to judgments based on their circumstances and needs. Concern for just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to protect workers from that influence.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s step from the designation power to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

  • Because Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” [1]. The service fills “any members not selected” [1], so the power arises when seats go unfilled.
  • Because The PRO’s support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” [2]. That passage gives no example or evidence about how such designations are made.
  • So The bill does place those appointments with a federal agency. The further step, that those choices would turn on political leanings, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The FMCS-published arbitrator code lists honesty, integrity, impartiality and general competence as qualifications for arbitrators and addresses voluntary arbitration; it does not set rules for how an agency designates panel members. The packet documents a 2025 executive order directing reductions at FMCS, which concerns staffing and not arbitrator selection. Sources: [22], [27].

points.title: It puts resources for pay and collective protection at risk through compulsory proceedings and new legal fights.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 It puts resources for pay and collective protection at risk through compulsory proceedings and new legal fights.

  • Because King and MacDonald warn that compulsory arbitration requires “complex and cost-heavy hearings” [24]. Steptoe identifies another expense: “Courts will be asked to interpret the new statute and define the limits of the arbitrators’ authority.” [16]
  • Because The lawyers identify a direct risk to workers’ income: “This approach will direct employer resources to litigation and potentially decrease the amount of wages and benefits an employer can provide to employees.” [24]
  • Because Imposing terms by law also gives opponents a basis to challenge union funding. King and MacDonald argue: “The government will be involved whenever an arbitral-created contract requires fair-share fees. All of those contracts will be open to attack in our courts.” [24] These are fees for representing workers who do not join the union.
  • Because Those fees support help for members and nonmembers. Labor-law scholar Ann Hodges explains that a fee clause “permits the union to charge a fee for representation to those who do not want to join the union and pay full union dues.” [17] Yet “the union must represent all the employees in the unit fairly and in good faith.” [17]
  • Because Workplace access faces a separate legal attack. King and MacDonald argue that “any time this bill imposed a contract with union access rights, it would take property and violate the Fifth Amendment.” [24] Their claim is that requiring employers to admit union representatives takes a property right without paying for it.
  • Because Fee lawsuits can drain resources even when they fail. Reviewing earlier cases involving public-sector unions, Hodges reports that they “impose substantial litigation costs on unions that could otherwise dedicate these resources to representing workers” [17].
  • So Compulsory hearings and new legal fights can consume money for wages, benefits, and representation. Challenges to funding and workplace access also put the tools of collective protection at risk. Protecting people with little individual power gives [NAME] a reason to preserve those resources and tools.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s letters overstate the legal defects, and referral need not lead to a full hearing on every term.

  • Because Referral need not lead to a full hearing on every contract term. Reviewing Canadian cases, Slinn and Hurd report that “it is common for the parties to settle the contract on their own before arbitration concludes, and sometimes even before it commences.” [8] Settling some terms can “reduce the time and cost of arbitration.” [8]
  • Because Hodges’s evidence concerns lawsuits seeking refunds of fees charged to nonmembers for union representation. Those claims “primarily seek retroactive application of Janus” [17]: applying that ruling to fees already collected. This record does not show the cost of challenges to this bill’s contracts at private employers.
  • Because Government involvement alone does not invalidate bargaining fees. In Hanson, the Supreme Court upheld financial support for private railway bargaining and held that the requirement “does not violate either the First or the Fifth Amendments.” [28]
  • Because Janus distinguishes bargaining with government employers from private workplaces: “In the public sector, core issues such as wages, pensions, and benefits are important political issues, but that is generally not so in the private sector.” [29] The letters’ argument about government involvement does not resolve that difference.
  • Because Cedar Point does not say that every right for union representatives to enter a workplace takes property without payment. The Court distinguishes access to closed property from “Limitations on how a business generally open to the public may treat individuals on the premises” [30]. The legal result depends on the access granted and the premises involved.
  • So Settlement can narrow the proceedings, and the fee and access rulings do not show the blanket legal defects the letters assert. This response does not answer the costs of hearings that do occur, or of suits that drain resources even when they fail.

points.title: It can hold back pay rises after a genuine deadlock, including in later contract talks.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 It can hold back pay rises after a genuine deadlock, including in later contract talks.

  • Because Under existing law, “upon reaching a good-faith impasse, the NLRA entitles an employer to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer.” [18] This means putting that offer into effect without union agreement after talks reach a genuine deadlock.
  • Because The bill instead requires parties “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [1]. Steptoe explains: “This employer obligation to maintain all current terms and conditions of employment extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.” [16]
  • Because The maintenance rule “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” [16] The bill’s route to a panel is limited to “an initial collective bargaining agreement following certification or recognition” [1].
  • So Where an otherwise lawful final offer would improve pay without cutting other terms, the bill blocks the employer from delivering those gains on its own after deadlock. Later contract talks have no arbitration backstop under this bill. Closing that route to higher pay puts low-paid workers’ living standards and chances to get ahead at risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: In a federal case, an employer proposed and a union accepted interim pay increases during first-contract talks. In early 2014 the employer gave no raise; employees testified that a supervisor said it was tied up in negotiations. The union filed an unfair labor practice complaint, and a settlement implemented the wage increase with back pay. Sources: [31].

points.title: It closes an existing route for workers to end unwanted union representation.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 It closes an existing route for workers to end unwanted union representation.

  • Because Existing law allows an employer to announce withdrawal of recognition before a contract expires, effective afterward, “upon receiving objective evidence that the union has actually lost majority support.” [32]
  • Because Workers use this route. A June 2025 report describes a Sunoco driver gathering majority support against the union: “Fifer opted to submit his petition to his employer, who withdrew recognition from the USW union in accordance with the Johnson Controls decision.” [33]
  • Because The bill requires continued bargaining “absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1]. Decertification means removing the union as the workers’ representative through a federal election.
  • So Clear majority opposition would no longer suffice for the employer to use this route; workers would have to await an election. That adds an obstacle to ending representation they no longer want. Just treatment includes respecting those workers’ wishes about who speaks for them.
points.con_html:
Response Requiring workers’ wishes to be confirmed through a secret vote does not itself treat them unjustly.

  • Because The bill preserves “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [1]. Workers retain the route to vote a union out.
  • Because The PRO’s own legal account calls an election “the preferred method for determining employees’ representational preferences.” [32]
  • Because A signature is not always a worker’s last word. Describing workers who signed conflicting petitions, labor lawyers explain that a secret ballot allows a final choice under anonymity, “insulating them from retaliation from whichever side they fail to support.” [34]
  • So The election requirement checks majority wishes through a private choice by workers, rather than leaving the employer to act on signatures. Just treatment includes protecting that choice for every worker. The PRO shows that employer withdrawal can be quicker, but speed alone does not establish that verifying the majority’s wishes is unfair.
