pages.description: H.R.5408 would require an employer to begin bargaining soon after its workers vote to form a union. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, the dispute may proceed to federal mediation and, if mediation fails, to an arbitration panel whose decision would be binding.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on June 9, 2026, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect As of June 9, 2026, bargaining law requires talks but “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1]. The bill adds deadlines and a route to a binding first workplace contract: “This bill establishes mandatory deadlines for parties negotiating an initial collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and provides for mediation and arbitration to finalize CBAs.” [2] Mediation means help with talks; arbitration means a panel decides the terms.

points.title: It protects a continuing voice for workers whose employer opposes their choice to organize.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects a continuing voice for workers whose employer opposes their choice to organize.

  • Because Delay can undermine that voice. The bill finds: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” [3]
  • Because Talks must start within ten days of a newly recognized or certified representative’s written request, unless both sides agree to more time: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” [3]; “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” [3].
  • Because The bill keeps the employer’s duty to bargain in place until an election removes the workers’ representative: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • So These rules strengthen workers’ chance to have their chosen group heard despite management’s opposition. Hearing people whose choice one dislikes puts acceptance despite disagreement into practice.
  • Because In racially mixed workplaces, continued union work gives people shared tasks across racial lines: “Union workers engage in collective action around issues of contract bargaining and workplace grievances.” [4] The study also identifies discussion with “explicitly anti-racist” [4] messages as part of unions’ approach.
  • Because Research following white workers over time supports a link to accepting Black people: “our panel analysis suggests that gaining union membership between 2010 and 2016 reduced racial resentment among white workers.” [4]
  • So Protecting continuing union relationships also supports a setting for cooperation across racial differences. This gives [NAME] a further reason to favor protecting that voice.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats a stronger bargaining role as acceptance of different people.

  • Because Existing law already requires employers and representatives to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith with respect to wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” [1].
  • Because The bill adds a starting deadline: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” [3], extendable by agreement: “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” [3]. It extends the duty: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • So The added rules concern when talks start and how long the representative keeps its bargaining role. Giving that representative a stronger role in negotiating work terms does not by itself show greater acceptance or understanding of different people. The PRO moves between these meanings of being heard without defending the link. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate branch on cooperation across racial lines.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The racial-resentment study concerns white workers gaining union membership between 2010 and 2016, not first-contract rules. The authors say that contact without explicit anti-racism strategies may not reduce resentment, and also state that unions facilitate discussion including anti-racist messaging. Sources: [4].

points.title: It gives opposing groups help in hearing each other and a shared way to settle disagreement.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It gives opposing groups help in hearing each other and a shared way to settle disagreement.

  • Because The existing system already allows voluntary mediation: “The FMCS provides completely free, completely voluntary contract mediation services to parties engaged in negotiations” [5].
  • Because Its role fits the problem: “In first contract mediation, a neutral third party comes in to help facilitate the bargaining process between parties that do not have a mature bargaining relationship.” [5]
  • Because After ninety days of talks, or a longer period both sides accept, “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3] The service must “promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [3]
  • Because If no agreement follows within thirty days of the request, or an agreed extension, the dispute goes to a panel with “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [3] If selection fails, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [3]
  • Because The panel’s decision must weigh both sides’ needs: “the employer's financial status and prospects” [3]; “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [3].
  • Because Its decision supplies shared rules even while disagreement remains: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3]
  • So Either side gains a legal route to help with a difficult conversation. If talks fail, each side has a place in choosing a panel that must consider their needs. [NAME] has a reason to favor this way of working with people despite disagreement.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO treats a route to settlement as added mutual listening without establishing the help or understanding it claims.

  • Because Mediation already exists: “The FMCS provides completely free, completely voluntary contract mediation services to parties engaged in negotiations” [5].
  • Because The bill changes access: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3] It directs the service to “promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” [3]
  • Because A March 2026 review reports: “According to FMCS’s website, only 58 mediators remain at the agency (FMCS 2026).” [6] It also records the agency’s own assessment: “FMCS’s leadership stated that FMCS needed at least 80–100 mediators to meet its statutory duties, and could only do so if mediation was held virtually instead of in-person.” [6]
  • So An added right to request help does not supply the missing mediators. This limits how much added help with talks the PRO can claim; it does not show that the duty would produce none.
  • Because The next step applies when “the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation” [3]. Then “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3]
  • So Choosing panel members and having economic needs weighed concern how work terms are decided. A panel can settle those terms while the groups remain unwilling to listen to or understand each other. Settlement alone therefore does not establish the mutual hearing and acceptance the PRO attributes to it.

points.title: A firmer route to first contracts helps workers secure enforceable acceptance of different identities and beliefs.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 A firmer route to first contracts helps workers secure enforceable acceptance of different identities and beliefs.

  • Because First contracts already provide tools for this. Kickstarter workers voted to “ratify their first collective bargaining agreement with their employer.” [7] Its terms say employment decisions “are not based on any protected status.” [8] The listed traits include “religion, creed” [8] and “political affiliation” [8].
  • Because Contracts give workers a way to enforce such rules: “Through procedures that address contract violations, union contracts can be used to hold employers accountable and compel them to follow anti-discrimination policies.” [9]
  • Because Contract terms can also adapt work to people’s differences. At Santa Fe Opera, workers won rules requiring “costumes, wigs, hair coloring, shoes, and make-up that are appropriate for a range of skin tones.” [9]
  • So For workers seeking these terms, the bill removes first-contract deadlock as a way to block the whole contract. It strengthens their route to enforceable protection from mistreatment for who they are or what they believe, and to practical acceptance of differences. That serves [NAME]’s value.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The toolkit describes selected negotiated results in professional workplaces. Kickstarter’s first contract was ratified without arbitration, its forum has no decision or bargaining authority, and its arbitrator cannot add to the agreement’s terms. The bill’s panel factors do not name these terms. Sources: [9], [8], [3].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [10], [11].

points.title: First contracts can establish lasting opportunities to understand different people.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 First contracts can establish lasting opportunities to understand different people.

  • Because Contracts have created regular discussions across workplace groups: “Union professionals have used their contracts to establish groups made up of managers and union members that meet regularly to discuss and address diversity issues.” [9]
  • Because Kickstarter’s first contract gives a concrete example: “To hold quarterly meetings during the work day with the participation of employees and management.” [8]
  • Because Those meetings expressly welcome different views: “Any participant may propose issues to address and invite employees who have a particular expertise or viewpoint to a meeting.” [8] Participants agree to “maintain a respectful atmosphere at all times.” [8]
  • Because Contracts can also require repeated learning about bias. Actors’ Equity secured a rule that “theaters will provide mandatory anti-discrimination and harassment training on at least an annual basis.” [9]
  • So By providing a route through first-contract deadlock, the bill helps workers turn proposals for continuing discussion and learning into workplace rules. Supporting these opportunities gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill because [NAME] values listening to and understanding people who are different.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: The toolkit describes selected negotiated results in professional workplaces. Kickstarter’s first contract was ratified without arbitration, its forum has no decision or bargaining authority, and its arbitrator cannot add to the agreement’s terms. The bill’s panel factors do not name these terms. Sources: [9], [8], [3].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [10], [11].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill would let an arbitration panel settle unresolved first-contract disputes with binding terms: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3] It would also keep the employer's duty to bargain in place until an election removes the union: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].

points.title: It bypasses contract votes that make negotiators answer to union members who disagree.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It bypasses contract votes that make negotiators answer to union members who disagree.

  • Because Contract votes give members a way to question and reject terms. UAW Local 600 explains that members have “a very powerful right to ask questions about any resulting tentative agreement and vote it up or down as you wish with your co-workers.” [12]
  • Because Rejection can return disputed issues to bargaining: “If the tentative agreement is rejected, the union may demand that the employer resume bargaining to resolve the issue(s) causing member rejection” [12].
  • Because In cases sent to arbitration, the bill makes the panel's decision binding without requiring a member approval vote: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [3].
  • So Members can favor a union yet oppose particular contract terms. Arbitration bypasses their existing route to withhold approval and press negotiators to answer their objections. [NAME]'s wish to listen to people who disagree gives a reason to preserve that route.
  • Note Selecting a panel member does not restore a vote on the resulting contract. The bill gives the union “one member selected by the individual or labor organization” [3]; the panel's majority decides the terms.
  • Because For workers in states that permit required bargaining fees, a contract can also make nonmembers pay for representation to keep their jobs. The Supreme Court describes agreements “requiring all employees in the bargaining unit to pay union dues as a condition of continued employment, whether or not the employees become union members.” [13]
  • Because This payment concerns bargaining representation. The Court limits compulsory nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” [13]. Federal law also protects state bans on agreements “prohibited by State or Territorial Law” [1].
  • So An imposed contract containing a lawful fee clause also makes workers fund a bargaining voice they reject. Respect for dissent gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added burden on workers who choose not to join the union.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not connect bypassing final approval or imposing bargaining fees to less listening or acceptance of dissenters.

  • Because The PRO's union example gathers members' views before final approval: “Our union’s bargaining process starts with a concerted effort to get feedback from you and your fellow members.” [12]
  • Because In that example, members also elect their bargaining committee: “Your local union bylaws contain democratic voting procedures for you to elect a committee to bargain on behalf of you and your co-workers.” [12]
  • Because Federal law protects members' right “to meet and assemble freely with other members; and to express any views, arguments, or opinions” [14]. The bill's binding award leaves those protections intact.
  • Because The union must represent dissenters fairly. The PRO's court decision describes its “statutory obligation to serve the interests of all members without hostility or discrimination toward any” [13].
  • So The final vote adds power to reject terms and press for changes. The PRO does not show that removing this power reduces listening through member feedback, protected debate, and an elected bargaining committee.
  • So Accepting people who disagree does not mean accepting their preferred terms. The PRO needs to show less hearing or acceptance of dissenters, beyond less control over the outcome.
  • Because The same decision describes representation “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit” [13] and limits compulsory nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” [13].
  • So A bargaining fee pays for representation that must serve dissenters too; it does not require their agreement with the union. The PRO identifies a financial burden, without showing that it makes dissenters less heard or accepted. A reason to reject compulsory payment needs a further link to this value.

points.title: It gives either side a route around reaching terms the opposing group can accept.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It gives either side a route around reaching terms the opposing group can accept.

  • Because Existing law requires both sides to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith” [1], but “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1].
  • Because The bill lets either side request mediation after 90 days of bargaining: “If after the expiration of the 90-day period beginning on the date on which bargaining is commenced, or such additional period as the parties may agree upon, the parties have failed to reach an agreement, either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [3]
  • Because After the “30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made” [3], unresolved disputes must go to arbitration: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [3]. The clock starts with the request, rather than the first mediation session.
  • Because Mediation helps the parties find a solution they choose. The federal mediation agency describes this feature as “Parties retain control of resolution” [15].
  • Because Compulsory arbitration creates a competing route. A 2008 legal analysis of an earlier first-contract arbitration proposal describes the danger that “the parties speak not to one another, but to the arbitrator.” [16]
  • So Failure to agree triggers the bill's route to imposed terms even after sincere, good-faith talks. A side expecting better terms from the panel gains a way around further compromise with the other group.
  • So [NAME] values listening to people with different views. That gives a reason to preserve the need for both groups to work through their differences and find terms each accepts.
  • Note Extra time requires agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” [3]. One side's willingness to keep seeking common ground cannot prevent the other from pursuing a binding award.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not establish that arbitration reduces efforts to understand the other side, and current law does not ensure terms both sides accept.

  • Because Existing law requires good-faith talks while stating that this duty “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1].
  • Because After good-faith talks reach a genuine deadlock, an employer can put certain earlier proposals into effect without union agreement: “an employer does not violate the Act by making unilateral changes that are reasonably comprehended within his pre-impasse proposals” [17].
  • So Keeping current law does not preserve a requirement that workplace terms win both groups' acceptance. Agreement on terms is also a different test from understanding the people proposing them.
  • Because The bill requires parties to “make every reasonable effort to conclude and sign a collective bargaining agreement” [3]. It requires the mediation service to “use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement” [3].
  • Because Research on Canadian first-contract arbitration supplies evidence against the predicted retreat from negotiation: “Despite this, FCA is not accessed frequently and it is even rarer for a first contract (in whole or in part) to be imposed. Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” [18]
  • So The bill's deadlines do not excuse efforts to reach agreement. The first-contract evidence challenges the PRO's prediction that a binding fallback weakens those efforts. One side's refusal to extend talks after sincere bargaining does not itself show less willingness to understand the other group. The PRO's reason depends on that missing link, rather than simply on the loss of power to insist on more time.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Canadian first-contract study reports that arbitration is rarely accessed and rarely imposes a contract. It also notes that Canadian applications require any work stoppage in progress to stop, a rule not explicit in the U.S. proposal it discusses. Sources: [18].

points.title: It puts local groups' distinct ways of working at risk of being overridden by people who do not understand them.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It puts local groups' distinct ways of working at risk of being overridden by people who do not understand them.

  • Because Construction bargaining reflects differences between places and crafts. The Associated General Contractors of America describes “local multi-employer bargaining structures that reflect regional market conditions, craft practices, and established area agreements.” [19]
  • Because The association identifies the specific risk: “outside arbitration panels unfamiliar with local construction markets could impose contract terms that fail to reflect the industry or local labor standards.” [19]
  • Because The bill lets a panel majority settle the dispute. Changes to its two-year award require both parties' consent: “unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [3]
  • So The bill removes the need for both sides' agreement before unfamiliar decision makers set binding terms. A local group whose practices are misunderstood cannot secure a correction through its objection alone.
  • So Listening to different groups includes taking their local experience and working practices seriously. The risk of overriding that knowledge gives [NAME] a reason to oppose transferring final control to the panel.
  • Note The panel must consider “the size and type of the employer's operations and business” [3]. That broad factor does not give the affected craft groups a right to reject terms that miss their local practices.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The panel includes one union-selected and one employer-selected member, and its decision must be based partly on the size and type of the employer’s operations. The FMCS-published arbitrator code says an arbitrator lacking specialized knowledge must decline, withdraw or request technical help, and should comply with a party’s request to visit a work area; the code addresses voluntary arbitration and is applied to agency rosters. A 2009 review says both parties produce evidence to the arbitrator. These warnings and responses cite no record of how arbitrated rules have fit particular workplaces. Sources: [20], [10], [3].

points.title: It closes an existing way to act on workers' rejection of a union that no longer has majority support.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 It closes an existing way to act on workers' rejection of a union that no longer has majority support.

  • Because Union representation covers dissenters too. The Supreme Court explains that the union bargains “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit over wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” [13].
  • Because At contract expiration, existing law allows an employer with timely, untainted proof of lost majority support to withdraw recognition—to stop treating the union as the workers' bargaining representative. The NLRB states that “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” [21].
  • Because The bill instead continues the duty until an election removes the union: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • So Even independently expressed rejection sufficient for that existing route would no longer end the bargaining duty. Workers would have to obtain an election removing the union before the employer could stop bargaining with it.
  • So Respecting people who disagree includes listening when workers reject a group's claim to speak for them. Closing a lawful route for acting on those changed wishes gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not show why confirming workers' rejection in an election gives their changed wishes less of a hearing.

  • Because The existing route gives the employer an option to stop recognizing the union: “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” [21]. That is an employer's power, rather than a vote workers can themselves cast to remove the union.
  • Because The bill makes removal depend on “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” [3].
  • Because Section 9 allows a petition “by an employee or group of employees” [22] challenging the union's continued support. If the labor board finds a question about representation, it “shall direct an election by secret ballot and shall certify the results thereof.” [22]
  • Because The PRO's own labor-board decision calls a board-run secret vote “the preferred means of resolving questions concerning representation.” [21]
  • So Workers can take their changed wishes to the board without depending on employer withdrawal. An election tests the workforce's current choice, including the views of workers who did not sign the petition. The PRO does not connect losing the employer's option to act without that vote to less listening or acceptance of workers who reject the union.

pages.description: H.R.5408 would require an employer to begin bargaining soon after its workers vote to form a union. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, the dispute may proceed to federal mediation and, if mediation fails, to an arbitration panel whose decision would be binding.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect The bill creates a path to a first labor contract that both sides must follow: “This bill establishes mandatory deadlines for parties negotiating an initial collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and provides for mediation and arbitration to finalize CBAs.” [1] If talks and mediation fail, a three-person panel settles the dispute: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [2] This changes the law in force on June 9, 2026, which “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal” [3]. The bill also requires employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2].

points.title: Faster first contracts bring enforceable workplace safety rules within reach sooner.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Faster first contracts bring enforceable workplace safety rules within reach sooner.

  • Because First contracts secure safety rules that workers can enforce through complaints. A study of agreements reached in 1987–1996 found that “55 percent of private sector contracts have grievable health and safety clauses.” [4]
  • Because These rules address concrete hazards. A study of 16 contracts from 2010–2014 found: “Most contracts detail the employer’s responsibility to provide and maintain protective clothing and equipment.” [5]
  • Because Unions also help workers report hazards without retaliation: “They bargain to improve safety practices, protect their members against retaliation for reporting a violation, or make complaints on members’ behalf about hazards” [6].
  • So The bill’s binding route to a first contract helps workers secure and enforce these safeguards sooner. Protection from hazards serves [NAME]’s aim to avoid injury and illness at work.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: Keeping existing terms during talks protects health benefits and safe working conditions from cuts after a bargaining deadlock.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 Keeping existing terms during talks protects health benefits and safe working conditions from cuts after a bargaining deadlock.

  • Because Existing law permits an employer to impose its last offer after a genuine deadlock: “When parties reach impasse, the employer may implement its final offer.” [3]
  • Because The bill instead requires employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2].
  • So The bill closes that route to cuts in existing health coverage, sick leave, and safety rules while workers await a deal. Preserving those protections serves [NAME]’s personal health and safety.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: A June 11 legal analysis reads the bill’s maintenance language as applying even after a good-faith bargaining impasse. Sources: [10].

points.title: Earlier contract-backed health benefits make medical care easier to afford.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Earlier contract-backed health benefits make medical care easier to afford.

  • Because First contracts secure health coverage. The first-contract study found that “first contracts establish, codify, and expand health insurance” [4].
  • Because Bargaining produces benefit gains. Treasury’s research review finds that “the higher rates of fringe benefits at newly unionized firms are the direct result of collective bargaining.” [6]
  • Because A study following workers before and after joining a union found them “more likely to have access to health insurance” [6] and “more likely to pay a lower portion of their healthcare expenses out-of-pocket.” [6]
  • So Speeding access to these contract benefits lowers a cost barrier to medical care. That directly serves [NAME]’s aim to prevent disease and protect health.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: Contract sick leave gives workers time for care and recovery and protects others from infection.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Contract sick leave gives workers time for care and recovery and protects others from infection.

  • Because First-contract research found agreements that “provide for some sick leave benefits.” [4] A study following workers before and after joining a union found them “more likely to have access to paid sick leave” [6].
  • Because Paid leave removes the need to lose pay to seek care: “Paid sick leave benefits allow workers to stay home and visit a healthcare provider when ill.” [11]
  • Because Staying home also protects other people. A U.S. study comparing states with and without sick-leave requirements found: “We find clear evidence that sick pay mandates reduce ILI infection rates at the population level.” [12] ILI means flu-like illness.
  • So Bringing paid sick leave forward supports treatment and recovery and reduces exposure to infectious workers. [NAME] gains a personal health reason as a worker, coworker, customer, or patient.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: The infection study examines state and city mandates under which workers accrue one hour of paid sick leave per 30 to 40 hours. Its population-level estimate concerns those laws, not contract leave. Sources: [12].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: Contract pay gains help workers afford the things that keep them healthy.
points.pro_html:
Point 5 Contract pay gains help workers afford the things that keep them healthy.

  • Because Bargaining raises pay. Treasury’s review concludes: “All in all, the evidence points to a union wage premium of around 10 to 15 percent, with larger effects for longer tenured workers.” [6] This compares union pay with comparable nonunion work.
  • Because The bill makes workers’ living needs part of a binding settlement. The panel must consider “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [2].
  • Because More income buys health protection: “More affluent people have more disposable income and can more easily afford medical care and a healthy lifestyle—benefits that also extend to their children.” [13] It also helps pay for food: “More affluent people can more easily afford regular and nutritious meals, which tend to be more expensive and less convenient than less nutritious, calorie-dense, high-carbohydrate options and fast foods.” [13]
  • Because Competition extends wage gains beyond union members: “Other workers see increases in wages and improved work practices as their nonunionized workplaces compete with unionized ones for labor.” [6]
  • So Bringing negotiated pay gains forward strengthens the means to afford care and healthy food, including through competition for workers. The reason for [NAME] is better health, with benefits reaching beyond union members.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: Treasury reports that the union wage premium is smaller for recent union hires and larger for long-tenured workers, and the 10 to 15 percent estimate is not specific to first contracts. Sources: [6].

Evidence note: A close-election study covering 1984–2001 reports small impacts of new unionization on employers, with wage estimates close to zero. The authors say unions have been somewhat unsuccessful at securing significant wage gains. It does not estimate the effect of first-contract arbitration. Sources: [14].

points.title: Negotiated schedules and rest periods protect sleep and recovery from work.
points.pro_html:
Point 6 Negotiated schedules and rest periods protect sleep and recovery from work.

  • Because First contracts include rules for work hours and schedule changes. The first-contract study explains: “These clauses are important because they provide workers predictability and control over their work schedules.” [4]
  • Because Contracts also secure rest. The 16-contract study found: “Most contracts include the indicators of paid annual leave, paid rest periods, and bereavement leave.” [5]
  • Because A randomized experiment that made schedules more stable in Gap stores improved sleep: “The intervention resulted in a 6-8% increase in self rated sleep quality among workers in treatment stores.” [15]
  • Because Federal workplace-health experts recommend rest breaks and adequate time between shifts to reduce fatigue. Their advice includes: “Consider allowing at least 10 hours between shifts, so workers can get 7–8 hours of sleep.” [16] They also advise: “Consider allowing rest breaks of 10 to 15 minutes regularly, such as every 1–2 hours during demanding work.” [16]
  • So Faster contracts bring forward rules that protect sleep and recovery. Those are direct supports for [NAME]’s health and safety during ordinary working life.
points.con_html:
Response The sleep experiment does not show that the cited contract clauses would produce its sleep gain.

  • Because The experiment tested “five practices bundled together in a package” [15]. These included “more consistent days and times of work” [15] and added staffing. Advance notice was not the difference between the groups: “Gap rolled out two changes company-wide: elimination of on-call shifts and increased advance notice.” [15]
  • Because The first-contract study describes clauses that “require the posting of schedules” [4]. Those clauses are not the package the experiment tested.
  • So The measured sleep gain belongs to the tested package, whose differences go beyond schedule posting and notice. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate route through contract rest periods and federal fatigue guidance.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [8], [9].

points.title: Contract rights give workers a way to challenge harmful demands and arbitrary treatment.
points.pro_html:
Point 7 Contract rights give workers a way to challenge harmful demands and arbitrary treatment.

  • Because The first-contract study found rules requiring a valid reason for discipline or firing, “thus constraining management’s ability to play favorites or to intimidate and threaten workers who challenge them.” [4]
  • Because These contracts also made disputes subject to “independent third-party review of disputes between management and employees.” [4]
  • Because Control over work and fair decisions matter for health: “Unions can address job control, decisional justice, and other work conditions that are associated with coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, musculoskeletal disorders, and stress.” [17]
  • So Quicker first contracts give workers tools to contest unhealthy demands and unfair treatment. Protecting that control over working conditions serves [NAME]’s physical and mental health.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: The review’s worker study linked self-reported union influence among 771 New Jersey health care workers with lower job dissatisfaction. It did not test first-contract timing or the listed diseases. Sources: [17].

points.title: First contracts in private hospitals provide a route to safer staffing for patients.
points.pro_html:
Point 8 First contracts in private hospitals provide a route to safer staffing for patients.

  • Because Such contracts set enforceable staffing rules. Austin’s Ascension Seton first contract required: “In the emergency department, at least one RN will be required to work for every four patients.” [18] RN means registered nurse.
  • Because A study linked understaffed nursing shifts to patient deaths: “staffing of RNs below target levels was associated with increased mortality” [19].
  • So The bill’s binding first-contract process brings a route to patient-protecting staffing rules forward. [NAME] has a personal health reason to favor that protection when needing hospital care.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [8], [9].

Evidence note: The first-contract study reports workload and minimum staffing in 7 percent of first agreements from 1987 to 1996, and says most employers oppose such terms and argue they are management rights. The Austin first contract followed two strikes, and one nurse credited the threat of another for its ratios. The bill’s panel factors do not name staffing. Sources: [4], [18], [2].

points.title: Binding settlement reduces the need for first-contract strikes that disrupt hospital care.
points.pro_html:
Point 9 Binding settlement reduces the need for first-contract strikes that disrupt hospital care.

  • Because Arbitration gives the parties a way to settle their first contract without a stoppage. Evidence from private-sector first-contract laws in Canada supports this mechanism: “One study found that these laws reduced work stoppages on first-contract negotiations in the private sector by at least 50 percent.” [20]
  • Because Hospital strikes threaten patient care. A study of New York nurses’ strikes in 1984–2004 found that “hospitals functioning during nurses’ strikes are doing so at a lower quality of patient care.” [21]
  • So Replacing unresolved first-contract disputes with binding settlement reduces a source of disruption in private hospitals. Avoiding that risk to care serves [NAME]’s personal safety as a patient.
points.con_html:
Response The Canadian estimate does not establish the claimed reduction in U.S. hospital strikes under this bill.

  • Because The working paper behind the estimate treats health care as part of the “quasi-public sector (health, education and public administration)” [22]. Its separate private-sector analysis uses “only first agreement work stoppages that occur in the private sector” [22]. The private-sector estimate is not a hospital-specific estimate.
  • Because The Canadian laws also contain a distinct rule: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop.” [22] FCA means first-contract arbitration. The study does not separate offering arbitration from this rule requiring strikes to stop.
  • Because H.R.5408 requires that “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [2]. It adds no corresponding rule stopping strikes when arbitration begins.
  • So The reported reduction comes from a different package of rules and is not an estimate for hospital disputes. This response does not answer the narrower inference that a settlement route can reduce the need for some first-contract hospital strikes.
points.notes_html:
Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified. It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: [4], [7], [5].

Evidence note: The Canadian first-contract study reports no statistically significant effect of arbitration on the duration of first-agreement work stoppages, alongside its reported reduction in their incidence. Sources: [22].

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html:
Main effect For first union contracts still unsettled after bargaining and mediation, the bill makes a panel’s decision binding for two years: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [2]

  • Because Current law requires good-faith bargaining but says it “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [23].
  • Because Members normally approve contracts under union rules. As Heritage explains, “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” [24]
  • So Arbitration bypasses that approval check. Workers cannot reject the binding first contract through their usual vote; changing it during those two years requires both parties’ written consent.
  • Note The union’s panel seat does not preserve members’ final say. The bill provides “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [2] A majority can outvote the union’s choice.

points.title: The bill removes workers’ approval check on safety rules that fail to fit their workplace.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes workers’ approval check on safety rules that fail to fit their workplace.

  • Because The panel can set “safety procedures, leave policies, and virtually every term of employment.” [25]
  • Because The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors identifies the danger: “arbitrators could be empowered to impose work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations” [26].
  • Because Workers bring knowledge needed to spot those problems. OSHA explains: “They also often know the most about potential hazards associated with their jobs. Successful programs tap into this knowledge base.” [27]
  • Because Approval votes let workers act on safety concerns. Reporting on Providence nurses’ rejection of a proposed contract in 2025, Northwest Labor Press states: “Oregon Nurses Association said the agreement failed because it did too little to ensure safe staffing levels or make wages competitive to help recruit and retain staff.” [28] The nurses were in renewal talks, which the bill’s arbitration would not reach; the example shows how an approval vote works, not a vote the bill would bypass.
  • So Bypassing approval removes workers’ final chance to block a binding contract over safety flaws they identify. Preserving that check serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: After a genuine bargaining deadlock, existing law allows an employer to make changes consistent with offers the union rejected; before that stage, rejection can return the parties to bargaining or support a strike. The Providence nurses’ contracts had expired, while other units in that dispute ratified first contracts. The Conagra report gives no amount or outcome. The Commonwealth Fund figures describe underinsured adults, not workers facing a given cost increase. The union selects one panel member. The passages read for these points give no example of workers rejecting a tentative first contract over health or safety terms. Sources: [29], [30], [28], [31], [32], [2].

points.title: The bill removes workers’ approval check on exhausting schedules that threaten safety at work and on the road.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill removes workers’ approval check on exhausting schedules that threaten safety at work and on the road.

  • Because The panel can “impose wages, benefits, schedules, and workplace rules for years to come.” [25]
  • Because Workers use approval votes to challenge such terms. WDRB reported that Conagra workers “rejected a proposed labor contract” [31] whose terms failed to address concerns about “forced overtime and double shifts” [31]. The report describes an existing Teamsters unit and a 60-day “cooling-off period” [31], which points to renewal talks the bill’s arbitration would not reach; the example shows how an approval vote works, not a vote the bill would bypass.
  • Because The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) explains: “Work-related factors that can contribute to fatigue include scheduling practices, such as night shifts or extended hours, that can interfere with sleep.” [33]
  • Because Fatigue creates injury risks: “Fatigued workers might take more risks that lead to injury or errors.” [33]
  • Because The danger reaches ordinary road users: “The effects of work-related fatigue can also spill over into personal lives and can impact public safety, for example when fatigued workers drive on public roads.” [33]
  • So In arbitrated first contracts, the bill bypasses this way for workers to challenge exhausting schedules before accepting a binding contract. [NAME] has a safety reason to preserve that check against work injuries and crashes on roads they use.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: After a genuine bargaining deadlock, existing law allows an employer to make changes consistent with offers the union rejected; before that stage, rejection can return the parties to bargaining or support a strike. The Providence nurses’ contracts had expired, while other units in that dispute ratified first contracts. The Conagra report gives no amount or outcome. The Commonwealth Fund figures describe underinsured adults, not workers facing a given cost increase. The union selects one panel member. The passages read for these points give no example of workers rejecting a tentative first contract over health or safety terms. Sources: [29], [30], [28], [31], [32], [2].

points.title: The bill removes workers’ approval check on sick leave that protects recovery and limits infection and injury.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 The bill removes workers’ approval check on sick leave that protects recovery and limits infection and injury.

  • Because The panel’s power includes “leave policies” [25], so it can settle paid sick leave without members’ approval.
  • Because Paid leave addresses pressure to work while ill. NIOSH explains: “Access to paid sick leave might reduce the pressure to work while sick out of fear of losing income.” [34]
  • Because Research connects paid sick leave with recovery: “paid sick leave is associated with shorter worker recovery times and reduced complications from minor health problems.” [34]
  • Because It also protects people around the sick worker: “Paid sick leave also enables workers to care for loved ones and can help prevent the spread of contagious diseases.” [34]
  • Because NIOSH also found an injury link: “workers with access to paid sick leave were 28% less likely overall to suffer nonfatal occupational injuries than workers without access to paid sick leave.” [34]
  • So The bill removes workers’ final chance to reject a binding deal over inadequate sick leave. Protecting recovery, avoiding infection from sick coworkers, and preventing injuries give [NAME] reasons to preserve that check.

points.title: The bill removes workers’ approval check on health coverage that leaves needed care too costly.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 The bill removes workers’ approval check on health coverage that leaves needed care too costly.

  • Because The panel can impose “wages, benefits, schedules, and workplace rules” [25]. These benefits include health coverage: the AFT lists “employer- provided healthcare” [25] among union members’ benefits.
  • Because Approval votes let workers resist higher health costs. The rejected Conagra proposal “would have resulted in higher health insurance costs” [31]. That vote came in an existing Teamsters unit, apparently in renewal talks the bill’s arbitration would not reach; it shows how an approval vote works.
  • Because Having insurance does not ensure affordable care. The Commonwealth Fund’s 2024 survey found: “Nearly three of five (57%) underinsured adults said they avoided getting needed health care because of its cost” [32]. Underinsured means having coverage that does not make care affordable: “their coverage doesn’t enable affordable access to health care.” [32]
  • Because People report worse health after cost-related delays. In the same survey, “two of five (41%) working-age adults who reported a cost-related delay in their care said a health problem had worsened because of it.” [32]
  • So Bypassing workers’ approval removes a check on binding health benefits they find inadequate. [NAME] has a health reason to preserve that check against costs that keep people from needed treatment.

pages.description: H.R.5408 would require an employer to begin bargaining soon after its workers vote to form a union. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, the dispute may proceed to federal mediation and, if mediation fails, to an arbitration panel whose decision would be binding.
pages.comparison: If this bill took effect on June 9, 2026, versus law in force then

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to favor H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Under the National Labor Relations Act as of June 9, 2026, good-faith bargaining “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [1]. For first contracts covered by that law, the bill lets either side seek federal mediation: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [2] If mediation fails, a three-person panel must settle the dispute with terms both sides must follow: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [2]

points.title: Reducing first-contract work stoppages protects national production, military support and medical care.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 Reducing first-contract work stoppages protects national production, military support and medical care.

  • Because First-contract deadlocks last for years. Research found that “a third of newly organized bargaining units still do not have a first contract after three years” [3].
  • Because A study of Canadian first-contract arbitration found: “FCA reduces first agreement work stoppage incidence by at least 50 percent.” [4]
  • Because The comparison uses a similar bargaining system: Canadian labor laws are “modeled on U.S. labor law.” [4]
  • Because The shared mechanism is a reason to agree before a panel takes over. The study describes this as “creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement” [4]. The bill supplies that binding fallback.
  • So The bill gives both sides a reason to settle through bargaining and a peaceful way out when talks fail, reducing the need to force a first agreement through a stoppage.
  • Because Disruptions reach beyond the workplace. Federal mediation helps prevent “strikes, lockouts, and other labor disruptions that can be devastating for workers and much more costly to the nation’s economy” [5].
  • Because First-contract bargaining reaches private military support work. Newly organized Amentum workers “provide critical maintenance and supply support for military helicopter operations at the naval installation.” [6] Their next step was clear: “Preparations are now underway to begin bargaining a first contract.” [6]
  • Because Defense suppliers' strikes threaten military equipment. CRS reported: “Boeing’s Chief Financial Officer in September said that the company’s machinists’ strike would affect the KC-46 tanker, a military version of Boeing’s commercial 767 freighter.” [7]
  • Because First-contract disputes also cause hospital strikes. New Orleans nurses “held a three-day strike Nov. 11-13 to protest the refusal of the hospital’s owner and operator, LCMC Health, to address concerns about nursing staff retention as part of ongoing first contract bargaining” [8].
  • Because A study of New York hospitals found evidence that “hospitals functioning during nurses' strikes are doing so at a lower quality of patient care” [9].
  • So Reducing first-contract stoppages protects steady production, military support needed to defend citizens, and medical care needed to protect their lives. These are direct interests of a secure, stable United States.
points.con_html:
Response The Canadian findings do not establish how much this bill would reduce first-contract disruptions, and Boeing is not a first-contract case.

  • Because The Canadian study examines first-contract arbitration, where a panel can set contract terms. It calls this FCA. The systems it studies include a rule that directly stops strikes and lockouts: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop.” [4]
  • Because Its estimate pools different systems: “There is not enough variation across Canadian jurisdictions in the use of different types of FCA to permit the analysis to estimate the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” [4]
  • Because H.R.5408 requires referral to a panel: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [2]. It supplies no express matching rule to stop strikes. A June 11 legal analysis identifies the gap: “The bill also raises questions about the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during these first contract negotiations.” [10]
  • So The study's explanation about bargaining incentives does not separate the panel's effect from the strike-stop rule. The PRO has not shown that the reported reduction carries over to this bill's different rules.
  • Because The arbitration process covers “establishing an initial collective bargaining agreement” [2]. Boeing's 2024 dispute concerned an existing contract: “After ratification of a new contract in 2008, employees approved two contract extensions in 2011 and 2014.” [11]
  • So Boeing illustrates the harm of strikes, not an effect of the bill's first-contract arbitration rule. This response does not answer the ordinary inference that a settlement route can reduce some first-contract stoppages, including in the hospital and military-support settings the PRO cites.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The Canadian first-contract study reports no statistically significant effect of arbitration on the duration of first-agreement work stoppages, alongside its reported reduction in their incidence. Sources: [4].

points.title: A binding path to first contracts helps care workers secure infection safeguards.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 A binding path to first contracts helps care workers secure infection safeguards.

  • Because A first contract turns organizing into practical protection. First-contract arbitration gives workers a “guaranteed path to get the benefits of a union contract” [5].
  • Because Those protections include actual infection safeguards. Longmont United nurses won “the first acute care private-sector contract for RNs in the state of Colorado.” [12] It included “Health and safety provisions to ensure nurses get the highest level of personal protective equipment when caring for patients with infectious diseases.” [12]
  • Because Protective equipment is part of infection prevention. CDC's guidance lists “use of gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, or face shield, depending on the anticipated exposure” [13].
  • So Binding settlement gives newly organized care workers a route to enforceable safeguards that an employer cannot block simply by refusing to sign any contract. Strengthening this way to protect care workers and patients helps the United States defend people against disease outbreaks.
points.notes_html:
Evidence note: Longmont United’s first contract was reached through bargaining under existing law. The bill’s five panel factors do not name infection safeguards. Sources: [12], [2].

Evidence note: A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration rarely departs from the status quo in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions. Neither tests this bill. Sources: [14], [15].

points.title: Protecting and improving pay and benefits helps the country withstand economic setbacks.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 Protecting and improving pay and benefits helps the country withstand economic setbacks.

  • Because The bill makes a contract's gains attainable and requires the panel to consider “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” [2].
  • Because Treasury estimates a pay gain from union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” [16] It also finds better benefits and work rules: “These workplace improvements contribute substantially to middle-class financial stability and worker well-being.” [16]
  • Because Treasury links unions' broader economic benefit to “reducing overall inequality.” [16]
  • Because The bill also protects existing pay during bargaining. It adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2]. This closes a route to imposing cuts: existing law gives an employer a “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” [17] An impasse is a genuine deadlock in talks.
  • Because Financial strength has a national effect. Treasury explains that reducing inequality strengthens households, “making these Americans less sensitive to negative income shocks and thus lessening economic volatility.” [18]
  • So Making gains from first contracts attainable and protecting pay during talks helps households withstand lost income. That strengthens the wider economy against swings caused by households' financial distress, supporting U.S. stability.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO’s income gain depends on a general union pay estimate that differs from evidence on new unionization.

  • Because Treasury's estimate concerns union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” [16] The bill's first-contract process starts “following certification or recognition of an individual or labor organization as a representative” [2]. The union–nonunion pay gap does not measure gains for workers forming a new union.
  • Because Gains from forming a new union differ from the general union pay gap. A study covering 1984–2001 compared workplaces where unions barely won or lost elections. Its wage results, drawn from manufacturing, were different from the general pay gap: “estimates for wages are close to zero.” [19] This is evidence that the measures differ, not an estimate of this bill's effect.
  • So The general union pay estimate does not establish the income gain from new first contracts on which part of the PRO’s stability claim rests. This response does not answer the PRO’s separate branch on protecting current pay during talks.

points.title: Settled terms give businesses a firmer basis for steady operations and investment.
points.pro_html:
Point 4 Settled terms give businesses a firmer basis for steady operations and investment.

  • Because The bill's settlement is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [2]. That gives businesses a known basis for planning labor costs.
  • Because The bill's sponsors explain the planning benefit of lasting terms: “Companies also benefit from the multi-year contracts unions negotiate, which makes budgeting more predictable and long-term financial planning easier to manage.” [20]
  • Because The panel must base its decision on the business's circumstances, including “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2].
  • So The bill brings a similar planning benefit through settled, lasting terms. More predictable labor costs help firms plan staffing, spending and investment, supporting steadier economic activity across the United States.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO has not shown that shifting labor-cost decisions to a panel makes those costs more predictable than under existing law.

  • Because At a genuine bargaining deadlock, existing law gives the employer the “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” [17] The employer can choose the costs of the terms it puts into effect.
  • Because The bill removes that option by requiring employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2]. A panel then chooses unresolved first-contract terms. Its duty to weigh “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2] does not tell the business what costs it will impose.
  • Because The ruling is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” [2], but the arbitrators “have no set time to issue their award.” [21] Those two years describe how long the ruling lasts, not when its costs become known.
  • So The PRO counts the duration of settled terms without comparing the uncertainty of a panel's choice and timing with the employer's existing control over implemented terms. It has not established more predictable labor costs, so its step to steadier investment and national economic activity fails.

directions.heading: Does this value give [NAME] a reason to oppose H.R.5408?
directions.main_effect_html: Main effect Current law requires good-faith bargaining, but “such obligation does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [22]. The bill adds a path to an imposed first union contract. After 90 days of talks, either side may request mediation by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS). After 30 days from that request without a deal, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [2]. Both periods can be extended by agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” [2]. The panel’s decision is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.” [2]

points.title: It adds compulsory work to an agency that protects essential services and already limits its caseload.
points.pro_html:
Point 1 It adds compulsory work to an agency that protects essential services and already limits its caseload.

  • Because Requiring first-contract mediation at either side’s request adds demand for FMCS help. Former NLRB chair Lauren McFerran writes: “This mandatory requirement would presumably significantly increase the demand for the FMCS’s services, as opposed to the current, voluntary system.” [5]
  • Because FMCS would also have to fill arbitration panel seats when the parties fail to choose members: “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [2]
  • Because The agency’s April 2026 budget reports limits on the groups of workers it serves: “FMCS limited its involvement to facilities that provide health care services with bargaining units of 250 or more members, and to bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction.” [23]
  • Because The bill provides no funding for more staff. The National Restaurant Association warns: “The FLCA also assumes a significant expansion in federal mediation capacity that has not been funded.” [24]
  • Because FMCS describes its role: “Our mediators work tirelessly to minimize and prevent disruptions affecting utilities, health care, public safety and security.” [25]
  • So New compulsory cases compete for the resources used to prevent disruptions to power and health care. That risks weakening the state’s ability to keep essential services running and protect citizens, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose the added burden.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not show that added first-contract demand would fall on urgent disputes rather than on other work.

  • Because Existing FMCS policy offers mediation in disputes “which imperil or threaten to imperil the national health or safety.” [26] Health-care mediation also carries an existing duty: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to bring them to agreement.” [22] The bill does not remove that policy or the health-care duty.
  • Because The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) already handles first-contract cases: it “mediates collective bargaining negotiations for initial contract negotiations” [25]. The relevant burden is the extra work created by the new duty, beyond this existing work.
  • Because The added panel appointments depend on disputes remaining unsettled. Referral follows only when “the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation” [2]. In Canadian first-contract arbitration, Johnson finds that “the threat of having a first agreement imposed creates an incentive for the parties to reach agreement on their own.” [4]
  • So The PRO’s sources describe more demand and service limits, but not how the agency would allocate staff among disputes. Existing priorities make displacement of urgent disputes a separate step needing support. This response does not deny that added cases would stretch a limited staff.

points.title: It exposes small defense suppliers to imposed costs that can put them out of business.
points.pro_html:
Point 2 It exposes small defense suppliers to imposed costs that can put them out of business.

  • Because The labor law being changed reaches defense businesses. The NLRB applies its national-defense test to firms whose “operations exert a substantial impact on national defense” [27].
  • Because Representative Walberg warns that imposed contracts could “mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain, threaten jobs, kill growth, and in some cases, shut businesses down entirely.” [28]
  • Because The Defense Department says small businesses “keep our military forces combat ready with critical parts” [29].
  • Because The department also warns: “Over time, a decline in the number of small businesses participating in defense acquisitions will lead to a reduction of innovative concepts, capabilities, quality of service and increased acquisition costs.” [29]
  • Note The panel must base its decision on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2]. That requirement gives a supplier no right to reject the costs imposed; the award remains binding under the rule above.
  • So An unaffordable award that closes a covered defense supplier threatens the supply of military parts and capabilities. Protecting those supplies serves [NAME]’s priority of a United States able to defend its citizens.
points.con_html:
Response The PRO does not support its claimed added risk of awards that a defense supplier cannot afford.

  • Because Walberg says contracts “could mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain” [28], but the cited speech does not explain how a panel applying the bill's financial rules would reach such an award.
  • Because The bill requires the decision to rest on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [2] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees” [2]. The panel must use the employer's finances and pay at comparable businesses when setting terms.
  • Because A 2009 review of arbitration that sets contract terms reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [14] This account of arbitration practice undercuts the unsupported forecast of unaffordable awards.
  • So A binding award and an unaffordable award are different claims. The PRO shows that defense suppliers matter, but does not show why this process for setting terms would make them more likely to close. Losing a right to reject terms does not establish that missing step. This response does not show that an unaffordable award could never occur.

points.title: It puts essential deliveries at risk through work and safety rules that do not fit the facility.
points.pro_html:
Point 3 It puts essential deliveries at risk through work and safety rules that do not fit the facility.

  • Because The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors warns that panels could “impose work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations, creating significant operational challenges and unintended consequences.” [24]
  • Because Distribution includes essential food and medical supplies. In its pandemic guidance, the Department of Homeland Security lists “Employees and firms supporting the distribution of food, feed, and beverage and ingredients used in these products” [30] and “logistics and warehouse operators, distributors of medical equipment” [30] among essential workers.
  • Because The guidance links these functions to “public health and safety, as well as economic and national security.” [30]
  • Note The panel must use “the size and type of the employer's operations and business” [2] in setting its terms. That factor gives neither side a right to reject a final rule that does not fit the site.
  • So Rules that obstruct safe work at food or medical distributors put essential deliveries at risk. Protecting those deliveries helps protect citizens and keep the country stable through crises, giving [NAME] a reason to oppose this added risk.
points.notes_html: Evidence note: The panel includes one union-selected and one employer-selected member, and its decision must be based partly on the size and type of the employer’s operations. The FMCS-published arbitrator code says an arbitrator lacking specialized knowledge must decline, withdraw or request technical help, and should comply with a party’s request to visit a work area; the code addresses voluntary arbitration and is applied to agency rosters. A 2009 review says both parties produce evidence to the arbitrator. These warnings and responses cite no record of how arbitrated rules have fit particular workplaces. Sources: [31], [14], [2].
